title: Purple Is the New Green Is Ube the Next Matcha
paragraphs: In recent years, the bright green Japanese tea powder matcha has become a global sensation, appearing in lattes, cakes and ice cream around the world. Now, many people are asking whether a purple ingredient called ube could become the next big food trend.

Ube, pronounced "oo-beh," is a purple yam that is grown mainly in the Philippines, where it has been eaten for centuries. Although it looks very similar to the purple sweet potato, the two plants are not closely related. Ube's bright purple color comes from natural plant pigments called anthocyanins, rather than from artificial coloring. Its flavor is mild, nutty and naturally sweet, with hints of vanilla and pistachio.

Ube has long been popular in Filipino desserts, such as ube cake. But in 2026, it began attracting attention around the world. According to Google Trends, online interest in ube surged globally from the end of February. It is now appearing in cafés in a variety of forms, including ube lattes, cheesecakes, macarons and ice cream.

Major coffee chains have also noticed the trend. Starbucks and Costa Coffee have added ube-flavored drinks to their menus in some markets. For example, Costa included ube drinks in its UK spring menu, and Starbucks launched ube beverages in India in August.

Social media seems to be playing a big role in ube's rise. According to a survey by the data company GlobalData, more than 60% of Gen Z and millennial consumers use social media to discover products with new flavors.

However, the trend may also have some downsides. Britta Klein of Germany's Federal Centre for Nutrition warned that when demand for a food suddenly increases, it can disrupt existing farming systems, and that this is now happening in the Philippines. In the first half of 2026, the Philippines produced about 5,660 tonnes of ube, an increase of 17% from the same period a year earlier.
Whether ube will become as popular and long-lasting as matcha remains to be seen. Some commentators believe the trend will eventually fade, while others think it is here to stay.
